title: Shaddad: The Platform and Its Job

blocks.text: This chapter explains what Shaddad is, which work it does for NASL's customers, and why NASL builds a Simulink/Simscape digital twin of it. Business and product facts come from NASL's public website (nasl-tech.com, Robotat by NASL) and from NASL's internal ROBOTAT architecture document. Technical values come from the model itself (`params/param_*.m`, `docs/architecture.md`, `docs/specs/*.md`). The last section maps each real subsystem to the model files that represent it, so that the rest of the report can be read with the physical robot in mind.

**Sources.** Public: nasl-tech.com (Robotat by NASL, Arabic page, translated for this report, accessed October 2026). Internal: `NASL_ROBOTAT_Architecture_2026-07-11_v3.docx` (ROBOTAT architecture, version 3.0, July 2026). Model: `docs/architecture.md` (decisions D1-D63), `docs/specs/*.md`, `params/param_*.m`, `docs/STATUS.md`. The business model, services and productivity figures are NASL's published claims. The digital twin does not verify them unless this chapter says so.
What Shaddad is

Shaddad is NASL's flagship heavy-duty autonomous (self-driving) ground platform. NASL describes it as the intelligent base for all of its attachments: it roams every row, scans every acre and carries the tool the task needs, and it is designed to work around the clock. The chassis is tracked and skid-steered. Two rubber tracks on road wheels are each driven by their own electric motor, and the vehicle steers by running the two tracks at different speeds. There is no steering linkage, so the robot can also turn on the spot by driving the tracks in opposite directions.

blocks.caption: The Shaddad tracked platform: red body on two rubber tracks with road wheels, front display, key switch, E-stop button, and a flat top deck with a rail. Source: nasl-tech.com.

blocks.text: {fig:F21_photo_shaddad.png} shows the platform. The front panel carries the display, a key switch and an emergency-stop (E-stop) button. In the model's mass layout the top deck carries the sensor mast and, when fitted, the sprayer tank, and implements attach to a front coupler or a rear hitch. {tab:tab_platform} lists the design values that the twin uses. They are model design values, not measurements of a delivered vehicle.

blocks.text: The job: services, not just robots

NASL's website sums up its position in one line: "We sell robotic agricultural services - not just the robot" (nasl-tech.com, translated). Shaddad is how NASL delivers that service. The commercial front end is Robotat, which the site presents as a company of NASL. Customers order operations through Robotat, and NASL's robots carry them out.
Robots-as-a-Service

items: **Order on demand.** The farm orders an operation, and the robot comes when it is needed.
**Variable cost.** Each operation is priced in Saudi riyals (SAR) per hectare per operation, so the cost follows the work done.
**Standardised performance.** Every service has a defined, measurable result.
**Fleet managed by NASL.** NASL manages the fleet.
**Success metric.** Manual labour hours replaced per hectare.

blocks.text: This model has a direct engineering consequence: the robot earns money only while it works. Availability, energy per shift, safe unattended operation and predictable work rates are therefore primary design requirements. The digital twin is built to quantify these properties ({sec:ch01_shaddad/Why a digital twin}).
Attachments

Shaddad is a carrier, and interchangeable attachments do the field work. The site names three. The twin models all three as variants selected by one variant control, `VC_IMPL` (0 none, 1 mower, 2 tiller, 3 sprayer). This single control switches both the mechanical load (structure domain) and the electric drive (power domain), which meet at a shared physical shaft port, `Impl_Shaft` (decision D9). The mower is a deck mounted at the front coupler, the tiller a rotor at the rear hitch, and the sprayer a tank on the top deck that feeds 8 nozzles. {tab:tab_attachments} compares the public description with the model.

blocks.caption: Attachments: public description and model representation
rows: Low-height cutting tool for orchards and vineyards; regular autonomous maintenance
Front deck, 65 kg; 1.00 m swath; 2 blades at 2800 rpm; cutting height 0.03-0.12 m; 1.8 kW drive limit
Precision soil tool that adapts to soil density in real time for an ideal seedbed
Rear rotor, 85 kg; 0.60 m width; depth 0.08 m nominal, 0.12 m max; 250 rpm through a 12:1 gearbox
Computer-vision-targeted sprayer; up to 60 % less chemical through plant-level spraying
40 kg dry + 100 L tank; 8 nozzles x 0.6 L/min at 3 bar; 24 V pump; detector p_d 0.90, p_fa 0.05

blocks.text: Each electric implement drive has its own controller (`impl_ecu.slx`). It receives the rotor speed command over CAN (IMPL_CMD) and reports back in IMPL_FB. The MCU drives the pump duty, the nozzles and the lift actuator directly through its outputs. Two public claims are not part of the model. First, the tiller does not adapt to soil density: its soil load follows depth, ground speed and a fixed soil specific energy (80 kJ/m³), and its depth follows the lift command. Second, the 60 % chemical saving has not been evaluated: the vision detector is an abstract per-plant detection model (detection probability 0.90, false-alarm probability 0.05).
Operations across the crop cycle

Robotat sells operations, not attachment hours. {tab:tab_operations} lists the operations offered on nasl-tech.com, their published frequency per crop cycle, the means that performs each one, and how far the twin represents it.

blocks.caption: Operations offered (nasl-tech.com) and their coverage in the digital twin
rows: Phase 2 sensors and perception (navigation, obstacles); pest detection not modelled
`VC_IMPL` 1; S3 endurance and S4 greenhouse missions
`VC_IMPL` 3 with `sens_spray_vision`; S2 slope with a full tank

blocks.text: The site divides the crop cycle into 13 stages: monitoring, tillage, land preparation, base fertilising, seeding, crop growth, weed cutting, pesticide spraying, fertilizer spraying, pollination, repetition, harvest and residue cleaning. The site counts 10 of the 13 stages as done by the robot today and marks harvest and residue cleaning as partial or not yet available. It does not say which third stage is excluded from the count; crop growth is a passive stage, which may explain the difference.
Where it works

NASL targets three environments, and each one has a matching world in the twin. The field worlds are built by `utilities/world_build.m` (with `world_scn_palm_farm.m`, `world_scn_greenhouse.m` and `world_scn_solar_farm.m`); all worlds are selected with the `World` option of `shaddad_params`: 1 flat_test, 2 slope_test, 3 palm_farm, 4 greenhouse, 5 solar_farm, 6 soil_strips. {tab:tab_environments} compares the published claims with the model worlds.

blocks.text: The greenhouse figures agree with each other: 25 houses x 22 min = 550 min, about 9.2 h. The twin uses the same 360 m² house as its greenhouse world. Scenario S4 takes the 22-minute claim as its time criterion (at least 95 % floor coverage in at most 22 min). An early hand estimate in `docs/specs/gnc.md` (section 2.7: 40 m x 9 m house, 0.9 m mower, 0.5 m/s) gives 19-20 min. The modelled 1.0 m swath needs fewer lanes and should be no slower, so the published figure is plausible. The full S4 simulation has not yet confirmed it ({sec:ch01_shaddad/Mission planning (Phase 2)} and {sec:ch07_phase2_preview/Current Status}).
Operating concept: three shifts a day

NASL states a work rate of about 0.9 ha per day across three operating shifts. The twin's power design is built around this concept (decisions D45 and D46 in `docs/architecture.md`). {tab:tab_shift} shows how the claim becomes design values.

blocks.caption: Shift concept and the energy design derived from it
rows: 4 h: 70 % working, 30 % transit, turns and idle with the implement off
0.9 ha / 3 shifts = 3000 m², about 3 km of cutting at a 1.0 m swath
10.95 kWh for a new pack; 8.76 kWh at end of life (+13 % margin)
At most 3.6 h at 50 °C ambient with dock air on, T_cell at most 45 °C (bench T-PWR-10b); BMS charge limit 100 A up to 50 °C
8 h planning value: 4 h work + about 3.3 h charge (10 to 100 % SOC) + 0.7 h transit, so 3 shifts per day
The dock supplies conditioned air at 30 °C; bench T-PWR-20 checks at least 3 shifts per 24 h
Palm 1.0 m/s, greenhouse 0.5 m/s, solar 0.8 m/s

blocks.text: The budget also explains a design limit. At 1.2 m/s the end-of-life energy budget falls 1.7 % short, so the palm working speed is set to 1.0 m/s. Continuous cutting at 1.2 m/s for a full shift would need a 16S4P pack (20.5 kWh, +32 kg).
How a deployment runs
NASL deploys in three stages. According to the site, most deployments are operating within 60 days.

items: **Map the farm.** A field team defines the exploration and treatment paths and designs the mission for the crop and the season. The assessment is free.
**Robots start work.** The robots run continuous autonomous patrols, and their sensors collect inspection data. Errors appear immediately, and everything is visible on one dashboard.
**Findings become actions.** Detections trigger work orders in the farm management or ERP system. Operators step in only when needed, and the loop from detection to resolution closes automatically.

blocks.text: Stage 1 has a direct counterpart in the twin. A field map is a JSON mission file in `scripts/missions/` (`greenhouse_std.json`, `palm_demo.json`, `solar_demo.json`). `gnc_compileMission` turns it into the mission plan that the guidance model follows: coverage lanes, Dubins headland turns, transits and the dock approach. Stage 2 corresponds to Phase 2 autonomy. Stage 3 (work orders, ERP integration, dashboards) is outside the model.
The Robotat app

Customers use Robotat to choose an operation and an area, place the order, schedule it and track it. The public site links an App Store app and the web address robotat.sa. NASL's internal ROBOTAT architecture document (version 3.0, July 2026) describes the current implementation as a full-stack TypeScript web application, not a mobile app. It is a marketing site and customer portal: visitors browse the products and services, and registered users book a site assessment and track its status. Each booking reaches NASL by WhatsApp and by email. The document lists the services as grass cutting, fertilizer and compost spraying, land cultivation and scheduled maintenance.

The digital twin has no interface to Robotat, to fleet management or to farm ERP systems. Its boundary is one robot: operator or companion commands go in, and physical motion, energy and safety behaviour come out.
Why a digital twin

Shaddad's business case depends on hours of safe, unattended work per hectare. Hardware iterations on a 469 kg tracked vehicle are slow and expensive, and for safety functions they are also risky. NASL therefore builds a digital twin: a MATLAB/Simulink/Simscape model of the whole robot, covering structure and tracks on terrain, battery and BMS, power distribution and the E-stop chain, the traction drives, the MCU firmware, the RC link and the sensors. The twin serves five purposes.
Design sizing

The twin turns the operating concept into component sizes and checks them. The 16S3P pack was sized for the shift budget and re-checked against the revised budget in {tab:tab_shift}. The pack mass (118.8 kg) then feeds the mass properties, which set the traction loads. The drive was sized for 600 kg, and the full sprayer configuration (609 kg) exceeds this by 1.5 % (decision D17). Scenario S2 drives that configuration up a 20° slope and checks slip, pack current, gearbox torque and motor heating. S2 was re-run after the fix pass (`S2_20261023_202915.mat`): 8 of 11 criteria pass, and the tilt warning, pitch and mean-speed criteria fail ({sec:ch09_results/Slope (S2)}). All domains share one parameter set: `shaddad_params` assembles `P` and asserts cross-domain consistency (for example sprocket radius, gear ratio and pack energy). A design change is therefore made in one place and reaches every domain.
Firmware development before hardware

`Shaddad_MCU.slx` (STM32H743) and `Shaddad_BMS.slx` (STM32G4) are not simplified stand-ins for the controllers. They are the firmware itself, written as Simulink models with IO variants (`VC_TARGET` 0 SIM, 1 HW with STM32 blocks). The traction ESCs are bought-in commercial controllers; `drive_esc.slx` is a behavioural model of their third-party firmware, which NASL does not code-generate or flash (`docs/specs/drive.md`, risk R10). Every CAN frame is packed and unpacked by the same codecs in simulation and on the target (decision D6). The firmware can therefore be developed and debugged on the desktop. The twin found four defects before any hardware existed, two in the MCU firmware model and two at the MCU-ESC interface:

items: **MCU firmware:** a missing `drive_ready` connection, which stopped autonomous mode from starting;
**MCU firmware:** an SBUS decoder that accepted corrupted frames;
**MCU-ESC interface (ESC model):** a torque-availability deadlock, so the robot never moved;
**MCU-ESC interface (ESC model):** an undervoltage latch that blocked restart after an E-stop reset.

blocks.text: All four are fixed in the build scripts (`docs/STATUS.md`, section 0). The two ESC findings define requirements for the real ESC: it must report the available torque `tau_avail` without the commanded limit fed back into it, and it may latch undervoltage only while its power stage is enabled. They must be confirmed on the chosen ESC at bench test.

Code generation and board builds are blocked on the current PC. Simulink Coder is licensed but not installed, and STM32CubeMX/CubeCLT and the GNU Arm tools are missing. The firmware models are verified in simulation only.
Safety logic verification

Safety functions must be shown to work under faults that are dangerous or impractical to provoke on a real vehicle. The twin injects these faults repeatably: front E-stop, remote E-stop (CH12), RF link loss, a silent SBUS line and random byte errors on the UART. As on the vehicle, the hardware E-stop chain (`Safety_Chain.slx`) works independently of the firmware. Phase 1 results after the fix pass:

items: **S8a front E-stop** at 1.19 m/s: STO after 15 ms (limit 20 ms), stop distance 0.213 m (limit 0.6 m); restart only after reset and re-arm.
**S6c, 1 % SBUS byte errors:** 302 corrupted frames rejected, no channel glitch, and the robot stays in MANUAL.
**S6d, 5 % byte errors:** controlled stop within one 10 ms sample of the RC link-loss detection, with no E-stop.

blocks.text: Operator training

Operators can rehearse the RC procedures on the twin before they touch the vehicle: power-up to STANDBY, arming, driving, the remote E-stop on CH12 and its reset on CH9, and the reaction to RF link loss. Arming (STANDBY to MANUAL) requires the mode switch CH5 at MANUAL, an arm-switch edge on CH6 with the sticks neutral, HV ready and the safety chain closed. `phase1_test_drive` runs these procedures as scripted drives (`'Plan'`, `'EStopAt'`/`'ResetAt'`, `'RCLoss'`) and shows the result in plots and a bird's-eye replay. For interactive runs, the `Operator_Console` dashboard (`VC_OPSRC` 2) provides sliders and switches.

In Normal mode the full model runs at about 0.3-0.5 x real time on this PC, and the joystick input (`VC_OPSRC` 3) is only a placeholder. The twin is therefore a procedure trainer, not a real-time driving simulator.
Mission planning (Phase 2)

Before a robot goes to a new farm, its missions can be planned and tested on the twin. The engineer compiles the field map, runs the coverage or patrol mission in the matching world, and checks time, coverage, cross-track error, clearance to palms, posts and panel piers, energy, and the reaction to obstacles and GNSS outages (scenarios S3, S4, S5 and S7). This is the engineering counterpart of deployment stage 1, and it allows the published productivity figures to be checked before they are promised to a customer.
Phase 2 is not yet validated and is outside the scope of this report; {sec:ch07_phase2_preview/Current Status} gives the status of its scenarios S4, S5 and S7.
What the twin does not cover

items: The Robotat app, fleet management and ERP work orders.
Pest detection, pollination, seeding and harvest.

Real-time or hardware-in-the-loop operation: Accelerator modes are blocked by Windows Application Control on this PC, and code generation is blocked ({sec:ch01_shaddad/Firmware development before hardware}).

blocks.text: From the real robot to the model files

{tab:tab_subsystem_map} maps each real Shaddad subsystem to the model files that represent it. Paths are relative to the project root. Controllers that will run as code on a processor (MCU, BMS, companion) are Model blocks with their own `.slx` file in `models/`. Physical parts and plant-side hardware are Subsystem References in `subsystems/<domain>/`. Every `.slx` file is generated by a build script in `scripts/build/` (`build_*.m`). A build script deletes and regenerates its files, so edits made directly in a diagram are lost at the next rebuild; change the build script instead.

blocks.text: The variant controls in {tab:tab_subsystem_map} are plain scalars in the base workspace. `shaddad_params` sets them together with `P` and `Ts`. Its defaults are the Phase 1 configuration: flat_test world, no implement, SIM target, Phase 1. The scenario scripts set their own configuration through `SimulationInput` and do not change the base workspace. To inspect a configuration by hand:

openProject('<project root>\Shaddad_UGV.prj');  % runs shaddad_startup
shaddad_params('World', 4, 'Implement', 1, 'Phase', 2);   % greenhouse, mower, autonomy
shaddad_params();                                          % back to the Phase 1 defaults
